lesson.title: The Wait: Understanding Blocking I/O
lesson.summary: Blocking I/O is the default behavior of socket calls: the calling thread simply halts until the operation finishes, which is easy to reason about but caps how many connections a single thread can serve.
lesson.body:
By default, when a program calls recv() on a socket and no data has arrived yet, the call does not return immediately with an empty result. Instead, the operating system suspends the calling thread entirely, removing it from the CPU's run queue and putting it to sleep until data actually shows up, at which point the kernel wakes the thread and lets recv() return with that data. The same thing happens with send() if the outgoing buffer is full, and with accept() if no incoming connection is waiting. This is blocking I/O, and it is the behavior every socket has by default, built directly on top of the Berkeley sockets API, unless a program explicitly changes it.

The appeal of blocking I/O is that it makes network code read like ordinary sequential code. A program calls recv(), and the next line only runs once there is actually something to work with. There is no need to check a return code that just means not ready yet, no need for a loop that keeps polling, and no risk of accidentally spinning the CPU while waiting. For a simple client, or for a server that only ever needs to talk to one peer at a time, this is often the right choice precisely because it is so easy to get correct.

The problem shows up as soon as a single thread needs to serve more than one connection at once. Consider a single-threaded server built entirely on blocking calls. It accepts a connection from client A, then calls recv() to read A's request. If client A is slow, perhaps due to a slow link or a long pause before sending anything, that recv() call simply does not return. The thread is asleep, waiting specifically on A's socket. Meanwhile client B may have already connected and be sitting there with data ready to send, but the server cannot get to it, because its only thread is blocked inside a system call that only cares about A. From the outside, the server looks completely unresponsive to B even though B's data is already sitting in the kernel's receive buffer waiting to be read. A single-threaded blocking server can therefore make forward progress with only one client at a time, in strict sequence, no matter how many clients are actually connected.

The traditional fix is to hand each connection its own thread or process. The main thread's only job becomes calling accept() in a loop and spawning a new worker for each connection, and each worker can then block freely on its own client without stalling anyone else. This works, and for years it was the standard design, but it means the number of connections a server can handle is limited by how many threads the operating system can actually schedule, and threads are not free: each one carries its own stack and scheduling overhead. That cost is the direct motivation for the non-blocking and multiplexed I/O models covered next.
